page.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
page.description: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. page.text_excerpt: Z Posts All posts A Critique of GPUI Nov 8, 2026 20 min read ui rust gpui signals benchmarks Recently, there has been a trend of more desktop GUI apps being built using native rust GUI frameworks. And there are now even well known electron apps getting official rewrites: Discord announced their app is being rewritten using GPUI.1 Meanwhile, a lot of the LLM-clones being published seem to choose egui. In this post, I want to explain why I am not sure those frameworks are a good foundation to build on. To put it plainly: I believe both GPUI’s and egui’s state models are dead ends for complex desktop applications. Both are impressive projects, and they have their place. Zed genuinely feels fast and nice to use, and I use egui myself for debug interfaces in bevy games. But I don’t think those frameworks should be the default choice for native desktop apps. I want to make two arguments: Every UI architecture ends up needing to know what changed and who depends on it, or performance characteristics will not scale. A framework whose state model cannot say so makes the application say it by hand, at the cost of whatever made that framework’s API semantics attractive in the first place. Once you admit you want that precision, components that run once, with signals and reactive holes, are the simplest API for it. Disclosure: I ported GPUI’s current Linux renderer to wgpu2, I built the benchmark harness used below, and I work on zgui, a signal-based Rust framework that appears in the charts. The only question that matters Raph Levien quotes Ron Minsky: “hidden inside of every UI framework is some kind of incrementalization framework.”3 A UI is a function of state, and state changes a little at a time. But if that function becomes expensive, you might want to start looking for ways to derive a faster way to update pixels on the screen from an incremental state change. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth. Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far. It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion, bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. page.text_excerpt: Sergey Kuhne Blog Tools How I'm fighting the AI Brain Fry NOVEMBER 8, 2026 If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one. You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab's reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM. Until you can't. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don't know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish. A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment. I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue. Here is how it actually works. The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there. An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine. What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff. The Principle posits that individuals in hierarchical organizations are promoted until they reach their level of incompetence, where they can no longer perform effectively and cease to advance. In contrast, our logic shows how these individuals may surpass this point and climb the hierarchy even further. Career-pressured individuals often take on high-risk, labor-intensive, or morally contentious tasks. page.text_excerpt: Linebender About Blog Wiki JIT bitmap text rendering for microcontrollers Raph Levien, November 7, 2026 I've been working on vic-2350, a re-envisioning of an 80s home computer on an RP2350 microcontroller board. Of course, such a project needs text rendering. Though bitmap fonts are now out of favor, I chose them both for efficiency and because, at low resolutions, I prefer the aesthetic of a crisp, intentionally designed bitmap font over the blurry mush of antialiased font rendering. They still have a niche, if a narrow one. I also wanted proportional spacing and kerning, again because I love the aesthetic of early Macintosh and its predecessors. Most text rendering in RP2350 projects is based on a fixed character cell, as achieving good performance is tricky. This blog post presents a technique for extremely fast rendering of bitmap text on microcontrollers such as the RP2350. I've implemented it as part of my race-the-beam renderer, but the same technique would work when writing into a framebuffer as well. The core idea is a JIT to generate highly optimized code on the fly for rendering a string. Racing the beam Around the mid-80s, a split was happening in the way computers displayed text. The established technique was a fixed cell size, and hardware that looked up characters in a font ROM on the fly as the image was scanned out to the monitor. The advantage was very fast update and responsiveness with limited hardware. A lot of terminals worked this way, as did home computers. The downside was the lack of flexibility. In particular, only monospace fonts were supported. The newer technique was a bitmap framebuffer, as pioneered on a line of computers originating with the Xerox Alto, continuing through the Apple Lisa, and finally becoming popular with the Macintosh. The framebuffer was vastly more flexible, but required a lot more computing power to keep updated. In the early 80s, you would generally watch text progressively render. page.title: Computing As Social Activity
page.text_excerpt: Computing As Social Activity Despite appearances to the contrary, computers are fundamentally social machines.1 We ought, then, to regard the use of computers as inherently social. Computing As Social Activity, or CASA, is a set of principles meant to align the ways we use, design and understand computers with social values that stand in support of communities, rather than work against them. Principles Computing is inherently social. Therefore, our use of computers should always account for community. Accounting for community entails concern for other people. Concern puts a person's agency before their utility. Discussion CASA is born out of the recognition that the development of computing has too often been unprincipled or antisocial. It should come as no surprise, then, that computing often detracts from the welfare of our communities. Here, "community" refers not only to formal communities (such as contributors to development of a piece of software, or members of an organization) but also to the informal communities that gather around some activity held in common, such as use of some particular piece of software, or participation in a social network. It includes geographically local communities, as well as dispersed groups bound by mutual concerns or interests. At its broadest, it expands to encompass humanity at large. Importantly, these principles are intended not only for software developers, but as a practical framework for anyone who uses computers. They are as applicable to interacting via social media as they are to software design, to home computing as to enterprise deployment. As such, these principles are deliberately structured as a corrective to approaches that reduce computing to the interaction between individual and machine. This is less a repudiation of earlier frameworks (such as FOSS)2 than an attempt to re-establish computing practices in values that necessarily precede technical concerns. Kirlian photography is named after Semyon Davidovich Kirlian and his wife Valentina who began their work with high voltage photography in 1939. You might even be reading this because I needed somewhere to point you. In which case, Hi! 👋 The Lippitt-Knoster Model for Managing Complex Change was originally written to describe a way of navigating large organizational shifts, but I’ve found that it’s also useful as a diagnosis tool for any kind of large and long-running project. After all, every project is a "change" in a microcosm. You might not have a complex organizational change to manage every day, but everyone is involved in long-running projects of some size and shape in a company. So that’s what I use it for, and it is useful indeed. The beauty of the model is that you don’t need an MBA or a special issue of the Harvard Business Review to explain it. It says that any complex project requires six components to succeed, and if one or another is missing, you’ll have some specific and corresponding failure. It can be summed up in a simple chart but also rewards you with some deeper insights as you apply it: Vision is the purpose and endpoint of a project. Vision tells you where you’re going and why. If the vision is missing, there will be confusion about what is being done and why work is happening. Consensus is a team's agreement and alignment around the vision. If a team lacks consensus, people will not want to do the thing and they will sabotage you. Incentives are the motivation or reasons for why people support the work and prioritize it appropriately.
